content:
The next morning, Ba Sing Se smelled of wet earth, steamed buns, and rain hiding in the gutters.

I found the boarding house exactly where Iroh had said it would be. The owner, a square-shouldered woman with a long braid, looked at the receipt, looked at me, and then looked at the weather.

“Iroh sent you?”

“Yes.”

“Then you’re probably harmless.”

“That is a generous assumption.”

“He has made worse ones.”

The room cost less than I expected. It was small, with a narrow bed, a wooden chest, and a window that looked over an alley where two cats were engaged in a diplomatic dispute.

“You can stay a week,” the owner said. “After that, pay on time or leave before breakfast.”

“Understood.”

“And no practicing firebending indoors.”

“I don’t firebend.”

“Everyone says that before something catches fire.”

I unpacked the few things that had survived the journey. The room felt temporary, but the bed was dry and the roof did not leak. I placed Iroh's receipt on the chest.

Then I went back to the Jasmine Dragon.

The door opened before I knocked.

Iroh stood on the other side with a tray balanced on one hand.

“You have returned the receipt,” he said.

“I was told there would be a second cup.”

“Ah. A person of principle.”

“A person of caffeine.”

“Even better.”

He moved aside. The tea shop was brighter in the morning. Sunlight entered through the windows and turned the steam above the kettles gold. The old men were already in their corner, arguing more quietly than yesterday.

Iroh led me to a table near the back. He poured tea from a green pot. This blend smelled of jasmine, mint, and something earthy.

“This is different,” I said.

“Yesterday’s tea was chosen for warmth. Today’s is chosen for thought.”

“What if I don’t want to think?”

“Then drink slowly.”

I did.

Iroh sat across from me. He wore a dark green vest over a cream shirt, and a few strands of silver had escaped his topknot. There was flour on one sleeve.

“You have been busy,” I said.

“The shop is demanding. It has an appetite.”

“For tea?”

“For attention.”

I glanced around. The shop was nearly empty.

“I can help,” I said.

Iroh tilted his head. “With the tea?”

“With whatever needs doing.”

“Do you have experience?”

“With whatever needs doing.”

His mouth curved. “A carefully constructed answer.”

“I’ve had practice.”

The door opened. A group of laborers entered, shaking rain from their sleeves. Iroh stood, and the moment moved with them. He took orders, carried cups, and remembered that one customer needed his tea without honey and another needed extra honey because he had not slept.

I began collecting empty dishes.

At first, Iroh tried to stop me.

“You are a guest.”

“I’m a guest who is sitting while you work.”

“That is one of the privileges of being a guest.”

“I don’t want it.”

He considered me, then handed me a tray.

“Very well. But do not carry more than you can manage.”

“Are you always this careful?”

“Only with people who insist they are fine while carrying too much.”

The remark was gentle enough to accept. I carried the tray to the kitchen.

The rhythm of the shop grew around me. I washed cups. Iroh brewed tea. Customers came and went. When the room quieted, he showed me where the clean towels were kept and which kettle had a temper.

“That one whistles when it is displeased,” he said.

“Kettles don’t have feelings.”

“You have met very few kettles.”

At midday, he placed a bowl of noodles in front of me.

“I didn’t order this,” I said.

“You also did not eat breakfast.”

“You’re observant.”

“I am old. Observation is one of the pleasures left to me.”

I ate. Iroh pretended to be busy with the tea shelf, but I noticed him glance over several times.

“I can pay for the food,” I said.

“You can pay by telling me whether the noodles require more chili.”

“They require more chili.”

“Then you have paid.”

He brought me a small dish. I added too much. Iroh laughed when I coughed.

“You did not warn me.”

“You asked for more chili.”

“I trusted you.”

“A dangerous habit.”

“You are enjoying this.”

“Immensely.”

The afternoon passed quickly. When the last customer left, Iroh locked the door and turned the sign to CLOSED.

“You worked an entire day without asking for anything,” he said.

“I asked for noodles.”

“You did not ask. I noticed.”

“You keep doing that.”

“I am trying to make it a habit.”

He filled two cups and carried them to a small table near the window. The city beyond the glass had turned amber with sunset.

“If you are seeking work,” Iroh said, “I could use help in the shop.”

I held the cup between my hands. “You’re offering me a job?”

“I am offering you tea, wages, and the opportunity to be corrected by a very opinionated kettle.”

“That sounds serious.”

“It is.”

“Why me?”

Iroh looked toward the street. “You worked without making a performance of your exhaustion. You noticed which customers needed space. You laughed at my jokes even when they were not good.”

“They were not good.”

“And yet you laughed.”

“I was being polite.”

“A valuable skill.”

I looked at the tea. The offer was more than money. It was a reason to return in the morning. A place where my hands could do something useful while the rest of me learned how to stop running.

“I’ll take the job,” I said.

Iroh's smile warmed the whole room. “Excellent.”

“You haven’t told me the hours.”

“They begin after sunrise.”

“That is not a number.”

“It is a beautiful time of day.”

“Iroh.”

“We will negotiate.”

He raised his cup. I touched mine to it.

“To the job,” I said.

“To returning,” he replied.

The words stayed with me when I walked back to the boarding house.

In the alley, the two cats had reached an agreement. One sat on a wall. The other sat beneath it, both pretending the negotiation had been their idea.

I understood the feeling.

The second week began with a broken kettle.

It had whistled too loudly, startled a customer, and cracked its own handle against the stove. Iroh held the pieces in both hands with the solemn grief of a man attending a funeral.

“It was not a good kettle,” I said.

“It was a loyal kettle.”

“It attacked the counter.”

“It was under pressure.”

“So are we.”

Iroh looked at me. “A profound comparison.”

“I am learning from the best.”

The new kettle arrived three days later. It was green, round, and painted with tiny red flowers. Iroh disliked it immediately.

“It has an arrogant spout,” he said.

“You cannot judge a kettle by its spout.”

“You have met very few kettles.”

The shop became busier as the weather cleared. Workers from the outer districts began stopping on their way home. A musician played in the corner for tips. Children gathered around the windows to watch steam curl from the cups.

I found myself greeting customers before Iroh did.

“You are becoming dangerous,” he told me.

“I remembered someone’s order.”

“Exactly.”

“They were impressed.”

“They will tell others.”

“That is how shops work.”

“That is how attachments work.”

The remark caught me off guard. Iroh was polishing a cup, but his eyes remained on me.

“You could say you are pleased,” I said.

“I am pleased.”

“You could say you want me to stay.”

He set down the cup. “I want you to stay if staying is good for you.”

“And if it is good for you?”

“That is not my decision to make for you.”

The answer was respectful. It also left me wanting.

That evening, after closing, I found a small parcel on the counter. Inside was a brass tea strainer shaped like a lotus.

“What is this?”

“A gift.”

“For the employee?”

“For the person who returned.”

I touched the strainer. “I only came back because of the job.”

“Of course.”

“And because the tea was good.”

“Naturally.”

“And because you were here.”

Iroh's smile became quiet.

“Naturally,” he said.

I placed the strainer in my pocket.

The following morning, I brewed my first pot for the shop without his help. I measured the leaves, warmed the pot, and poured slowly. The tea was balanced. The scent filled the room before the doors opened.

Iroh tasted it.

“Well?” I asked.

He closed his eyes as if considering a difficult philosophical question.

“It is acceptable.”

“Acceptable?”

“Very acceptable.”

“You are impossible.”

“You have said this before.”

“I will keep saying it.”

“Then I will keep improving.”

He poured himself another cup.

The work became mine in small ways. A shelf. A recipe. A customer who came to speak with me. A chair moved into the corner because I noticed the afternoon sun bothered one of the old men.

Iroh noticed all of it.

I noticed him noticing.

Somewhere between the first cup and the closing bell, the job became a reason to remain.
